Patoua?

I'll say, I'll say, I'll say, from God, I'll tell you, You might know some German Spanish songs too. Oh. Yeah, let's get it. It'll be good. Hello. Do you remember the song of Haiti, of Revolution? Uh-huh. Haïtien? Haïtien? Oui, la chanson Haïtien.

Tout Haïtien depuis plus de onze ans T'a fait souffert de la plus grande misère Manger tes chers, pas tes gagner l'argent La fin t'es tuée déjà beaucoup de mer En bas, sal bas, enfin bénissant le Seigneur Y'a fait partir fausser par l'ordre de Renard Bon Dieu dans ciel pour finir l'injustice De ces hommes de crime et de malice Qui ont voulu qu'au général vainqueur J'ai fait arriver pour finir nos malheurs En bas la croix d'honneur, abat le gouverneur En bas la couronne sans faire mourir personne That's a nice song.
Oh, c'est très intéressant. Where did you get that song from, you know? C'est à nous ?

I went to C'est Domingue Ha, ha, ha, ha Oh, my grandmother and mother, you know And we sang all the time I just cannot remember now Now that I would need You see, but it's nervousness, I guess Because I used to sing all the time All the time, all the time Till the neighbors would ask me If they say, oh, I hear you They always hear me say, oh, mon fin But they never hear me say, I was tired I hear you sing, sing, sing, sing, sing, sing Well, I say, mon pas fin, mon jamais fin And now, enfin, getting back
Your grandmother, was she in Santo Domingo? Was your grandmother in Santo Domingo also?
No, my grandmother wasn't from Santo Domingo My great-grandmother, my great-grandmother Was from Senegal
Oh, Senegal
Senegal See, with Senegalian That's how we knew so many of them songs, you see And just now, because I want to remember my kids

In Senegalia?
In Senegal

Well, you see, she was my great-grandmother Was only eight years old when she was brought here So she don't remember, but very little She remember her father's name, Drosin Prince Prince Drosin Prince was his name And her mother then was called Zaire But her, she was only eight years old when they brought her here To the Senegalia in Africa, ain't it? On the border of the French, somewhere around there And they had an old man in the yard, they called Paraco He was the only one that spoke that Senegal language And he would translate it to her master But I don't remember my great-grandmother, you know
You don't remember any songs that they had?

Oh yes, oh yes Do you remember any songs? I used to Because my great-great-grandmother My great-grandmother Well, then she knew her mother would show her some of the songs That she could remember from her home And she'd sing it to us children

Let's see. The purgatory, the chrétiennes. There is also a song from Mary Madeline where she goes to the temple and Christ is not there, and she goes to the garden and he is a gardener. Have you heard that? What? The resurrection of the Christ. Can't remember.
Can't remember.
I wanted to ask you about some Senegalese words too. You told me Avadra was one, wasn't that one? How do you say good for nothing in Senegalese?
In what? Senegal. Avadra. Avadra is good for nothing. What about Good Morning?
Good Morning.
Good Morning.
Good Morning.
Salikam Seram.
Would those be in any of the songs? Would those words be in any of the songs?
No, never. I don't remember. But I know the Good Morning is Salikam Seram. And how is everybody here? It's Pelemete Dumbaya Kayaka.
Do you remember any of the songs that went with some of the dances like the Bambuma or the Kalinda or the Kungjain?
Don't say Kalinda.
Oui, you can you sing a little about that? Don't say Kalinda, Bujun, Bujun. Mr. Pila or Cops. I'm going to hear something. I'm going to hear something.

I know, tous les jours dimanche, that's creole. Tous les jours dimanche, it's coming sometime. Tous les jours, c'est fait. Tous les jours, t'embouillaka yavaka. Ça n'a fait pour ça. As much as I know, I can't remember. Just cannot remember.

What kind of Mardi Gras song? That's a Mardi Gras song. That's a what kind of Mardi Gras song? That's a Mardi Gras song. Did you ever try to play those songs your mother was singing on your clarinet when you were younger? No, no, no. What? I wondered if George ever tried to play any of those songs when he'd hear you sing them, and you picked up your clarinet if you used to practice on them.
No, because you see, I would sing when I was putting him and my other son, Sidney, and them, but they were babies almost.
What sort of songs did you used to sing when you were putting them to sleep?
Oh, anything would come to my mind.
Do you remember the names of some of the songs or a little bit of some of them?
I remember Le Dr. Noir I used to sing and Fais du Dau.
Sing a little of, uh,
Tous.
Yeah.

Tous les jours dimanche, tous les jours c'est fait, tous les jours tombeau dans car à nous, ça n'a fait pour ça. Can you sing? Can you sing a little of that? Yeah, I used to sing that for them, yes. Sing a little bit of it now, if you will. Well, I just sang tous les jours c'est fait, tous les jours dimanche.
You spoke it, you didn't sing it, you spoke it.
I did sing it. Oh, yes. And I just cannot remember, and gracious knows I used to sing, sing, sing to my children to put them to sleep.

I have, uh, some recordings of, uh, or a couple of people who are in the same general background, you are, and, uh, next time I come, I'd like to play you some, uh, tapes of some, uh, French singers. They're younger than you are, but they know some of the same songs.
Yes.
They'll probably refresh your memory, and you'll probably remember some things.
You see, of course, now, I forget, I'm old.
I bet you remember some Mardi Gras songs. I bet you do. Mardi Gras?

Mardi Gras songs. Well, uh, let's see if I can remember that song Tati used to sing. Fum, fum, quitte mo balikala, a je fum abadra, that's no good for nothing. Fum, fum, quitte mo balikala, a je fum abadra, tu barrasé moi. Fum, fum, quitte mo balikala, a je fum abadra, tu barrasé moi. Well, that's Mardi Gras song.
Could we get a translation of that, since it's part real and part does something about it? How does that go in English? What would the words be? Say, what would the words be in English?
Hmm?
What would the words be in English? V. What would the words be in English?
In English?
Try to say in English. What would it, how would it go, what would it mean in English?

Oh, well that means, woman, woman, let me sweep this balikala, balikaya is the house. Yeah. Woman, woman, let me sweep the house. Woman, woman, good for nothing, you're good for nothing. You embarrass me. Woman, woman, dear following a group of Mardi Gras. But not now. I wouldn't make a step now to see Mardi Gras. No, I wouldn't.
You're not missing much. What was it like in the old days?

Oh, they'd sing all them songs that you're asking me about. They'd sing, they'd dance, the dance of the, you know, Creole dance. And they'd skip. And they'd dress like, well, if there was a bunch of Indians, well, then they would dress like Indians. Now they don't dress like Indians. They would dress like real Indians, with them blue dress and a yellow strip, you know, bias on the dress. Oh, yes. A little short waist. And the hair just tied, what they call it, pony now, pony. Pony tail. Pony tail. Yeah. Well, that's the way the Indians, the real Indians used to just have their hair tied like that.
Well, did any of the songs they sang come from Haiti or San Domingo?
Well, I don't, yes, I guess so.

Do you remember the names of any of the songs which came from Haiti or San Domingo, the Indians sang? I think some of the Creole songs undoubtedly came from Haiti. Yes. Because that's the language they speak, you know, Creole, it's Creole.

A while ago, Dave, before you came, we were speaking about the Indians and how they dressed. Yeah. And I was telling them children when I was in my teens that I would go to ball because we didn't, girls didn't run around like they do now. It was a pleasure then to look at the Indians. They were dressed like real Indians. They had that basket on the back, you know, and they sat on the floor and they'd eat the cowpies. I believe it was jambalaya. Jambalaya congri. It sat on the floor. But now the Indians, they've got all kinds of stones and things on the, not Indian enough.
You want a Coke or anything? Yes, I like a Coke. You want a Coke? Yes. All right, if you have something. Maybe I'll take that instead of a Coke. I don't know. I don't drink that.
If you make peep.
Yeah.
You know how they call that? In Creole, peep. Peep. Peep.
Peep. Pipe. Oh, pipe.
Peep.
Peep, yeah. Uh, what about the Indians? Did you hear any real Indians sing, Yabba?
The Indians?
The real Indians that were here.
Oh, I don't know. They didn't, the real Indians didn't bother. You know, real Indians, they don't talk much. Oui, no. Ma palais. But, uh, they didn't bother about Mardi Gras and things like that.
Well, where did you see the real Indians in those days?

At my grandmother's. When I was a child, she always had Indians that would come from Bafouca and I don't know where across the lake there. And she, when they'd come, they used to be at that market they called Lahal Sovar, Indian market. It's Bayou Road on the other side of the road. No, on this side of the road. And when they was too far from my grandmother, they'd sleep in the, in the yard inside the, what's the name? But when they was closer to my, my grandmother's place, they would come home. Sometimes there'd be three, four of them. And she'd just leave them lay asleep there. And give them coffee. They had one they called Catherine. And she'd give them coffee in the morning. They, Catherine, to Paulie, coffee. Oui. She'd give them coffee. The minute they take the left, the last drop, ma palais. They'd tell her, I'm going. Yes, I saw some real Indians.
Have you ever heard any songs about slavery? Songs of slaves or songs about wanting to be free?
No, that song of St. Domingo is about wanting to be free.
Tell us, what was the background of that song?
Oh, I could never tell you.
Can you try it off a minute? Can you remember a Fé Dodo? Let's see.
Fé Dodo, call un mon petit frère. Fé Dodo, tu as du lolo. Maman est en haut, papa est en bas. Fé Dodo. But did something come after that Fé Dodo? I can't remember now.

Well, next time I come, I'll bring some, the words of quite a few old French songs. And I'll, well, give you a few of them to refresh your memory. Probably if you get a little bit of them, you'll remember more.
It's not so long that I gave a young man, Villery. He had a box somewhat like that. And I was at the home. A la Sive des Vieillards, you know, old folks home.
Oh, yes.
And I gave him plenty of songs. Of course, I was younger than I am now. I could remember.
I wonder who that was.
His name was Jacques Villery.
Jacques Villery.
Mm-hmm. And he came one day at the home. And the mother superior says, call me and call two or three old Creoles in there. And we all gave songs. And now I just can't remember nothing.
What happened to him? Is he from here, Jacques?

He this young man? Yes. Oh, yes. His mother was a Miss Lanus. And his father was a Mr. Villery. Creole. Creole, born from here. And he was a very young man. But he went on with, these things were just beginning to come out, I believe.
Mm-hmm.
Yes, his name was Jacques Villery.
Well, I think he may still be around in town. That name is somehow familiar. Oh, is it familiar? The Villery's live in the French Quarter, some of them.
Mm-hmm.
The Villery's live where you used to live, nearby, huh?
Oh, yes. Oh.
Where do they live? They live on, uh...
Oh, it's a rampart. There was one Villery, rampart, and Esplanade.
Well, that's a drug store.
The druggist, yes. Are they relatives? Well, that was his nephew.
Oh, we can locate him then, huh? Yeah, that'll be interesting if he still had a...
That was his nephew, his brother's son. His name was Jacques. Mm-hmm.
Alice Zeno, January the 25th, 1960, Reel 2. What did you say? I couldn't even understand that.
You like your pipe. That means you like your pipe.
Oh, that's right. I only made some peep.
Little M.S. op, that's Creole.
How do you say automobile in Creole?
Projet mobile. Projet.
I can't understand that. Projet?
Projet.
Projet. Projet by We wanted to ask you about some of the dances too. Did they do the buck and wing? Did you ever see that?
Buck and wing? Oh, no. I don't know how to do that. In my days, they didn't have polka, masurka, vals, and cadre.
What about kalenda?
What's that?
Kalenda? Dancer kalenda?
Dancer ça, ça c'est chanson. But they didn't dance yet. No, they had polka, masurka, vals, and cadre. Vals is waltz, you know, what you call waltz.
What about the bamboula?
Bamboula? Mm-hmm. That's Creole. That's African dance. That's an African dance.
Mm-hmm.
Bamboula, c'est African.
How was that danced?
Well, they hold a dress, you know, and it's just their foot, and they had the horse, jarboun. That's what they made the music out of. Oh, yes.

Uh-huh. Well, last fall, you were telling us about those dances when that man from New York, Marshall Stearns, was here. And you mentioned you'd seen some dances in the old Congo Square. What kind of dances did they have there? On the Congo Square?
Danse Creole. Creole dance. Can you see this picture? Is there enough light here?

This is an old picture that we found that says Congo Square. I can't tell which direction that's looking or anything. Do you have enough light on that to see it? Turn the light on there. They have a lot of trees there.
And there's some building.

That's where the auditorium is now. But I don't know which way of the living. It's not the auditorium. Did it look like that? Do you know any time when it looked about like that, those trees? Those trees, yes. But this I don't remember.
But this, I don't remember that.
That building, you don't remember?
No. That, yes.
Did they have anything in the square in those days at all?
They had what?
What did they have in the square? Did they have any buildings?
No, no. They didn't have nothing in the square. Nothing but the trees. And there where they would go, there where they would go and dance, Creole dance.
What? Do you remember what they sang when they danced? Was there a song about when the potato is cooked, we will eat it? Con la patate, something, nous mangeons, comme ça.
Did you just give me a glass? No, I got my window glass.
I don't remember. Mais tout nard, les yers, oui.
Did you do a whiskey? Or when I give you a bottle of coke, you get another bottle. Another glass there. I don't know. Yeah.
They used to dance, Zolipon, on the square.
Zolipon?
Zolipon.
What is that?

That's a dance. They dance, they hold a dress. Zolipon, Zolipon Mambo. Zolipon, gardez comme l'icard. Zolipon, ah, Zolipon Mambo. And then they put a bottle and they put over it like that. They say, Sayamaku Pesa. Sayamaku Pesa. That was some African song, I suppose. By damn trees. Well, let's give you to Mr. Russell.

That's an old picture we got from Raymond Burke that he found someplace. That's Congo Square. I don't know what that building is. In your mother's time, she said there was no building there. That might be on the edge of the square, too. It might be even on that street.
Yes, it is, because Congo Square was the... Congo Square didn't have no house around.
Do you remember when there was an old parish prison back up there, too? Yes. Before my time. Yeah. You don't remember that?
No, I don't remember that. Well, you remember who killed the chief, I bet.
Mm-hmm.
You remember when they killed the chief?
I guess so. Tennessee.
Who killed the chief?
I guess so. I remember that.
It was in March. Straight through All-East Street. Straight through? Yeah. It was in March?
Wasn't it in March? Well, I don't remember. Yes, it was. It was, no.
What's going on here?
Sydney. Sydney.
Yeah, because Sydney had been around town.

Sydney would be 65, and Sydney was 63 years ago. Yes, indeed. We had plenty of dagoes home. When they were chasing them, you know, to kill them, on the counter, they killed their chief. They were afraid. So whoever was charitable enough, they were dying of fright, would let them in. We had three at home.
You let them stay in your house, huh?
Hmm?
They were hiding in your house.

Yes, whoever was charitable enough, because one man, all didn't kill that one man. Yes, it was on a Friday in March. Friday, I believe it was. Either Friday or Wednesday. It was very, very windy, that day.

They even have a song about that, but I can't get it. It's called The Downfall of a Lion. And they used to sing that around James Alley, if you know where that is. That's up in the, what, the Third Ward or the Second Ward?
Back to the Third Ward, I think. I don't know. Third Ward. Third Ward, yeah. It's in the battlefield.
Police. Machika.
I wondered some more about those dances at the Congo Square. How often did they have those? Do you remember?

Oh, well, you see, the colored people would go there whenever they got ready to give their dance. They'd go and put the bière creole, creole bière. They'd make it with the pineapple hull, you know, and the apple. They sell that cider, I believe they call it now.
It's all outdoors, then.

They'd go at the Congo Square there, and they'd put their little table there, and they'd give you a, settle your glass for a nickel. The nickels wasn't like they are now. The nickels had just like strips like this, and a big five on the other side.
What kind of music did they have for those dances?
The mouth, that's all.
The sing. The sing.
The sing.
Any drums, or?
Well, sometimes they'd have jabounmule, as they call it. Mule jabounmule.
Oh, yes.
I've seen those.
They use those in Cuba now.

Yeah, yeah. They use them in Cuba. Well, sometimes they'd have them. And if they didn't have that, they'd take tin plates and spoons and make music out of that. But most of the time, it was their mouth. There were the sing. Jolipon. Jolipon Mambo.
Pouven vous chanter ça?
Jolipon, Jolipon Mambo. Jolipon Coferto Carré comme ça. Jolipon, ah, Jolipon Mambo. And it keep up with their feet.
Did anybody charge money to get to those dances?
No, no, no money. Anybody could go in there, because many times I got a money beaten for running off to go see those Creole dances at the Congo.
Was the Globes Hall built there?
Not around there, no. It was just from St. Claude to Ramport, from St. Peter to St. Anne.
No Globes Hall in those days.
No house, no.
Globes Hall, the Globes Hall.
Hein?
Was the Globes Hall around that neighborhood there?
Globe Hall was at the corner of St. Peter. Well, that was in the neighborhood.
That's in that neighborhood.
St. Pierre and St. Claude. St. Claude.
And it was up in those times, Globes Hall. Yeah, because I had an opportunity to play the Globes Hall myself when they had a theater.
I wonder what they did with Globes Hall.
And then they made a boxing arena. And then they turned it into a broom factory. My two first children was born right in that neighborhood.
And you think they tore it down about? Around about 20...
Around about 27, 28 something. That's like... Oh, yeah, they're tearing everything down now. Want some coffee, Mom?
No, Lord.
I just wondered if those dances were something for the tourist people to go to see? Or did any white people go around to watch it?

Yes, indeed. By the drove, white people would go. It was really nice. It was comical, you know. And it really was nice to see them people dancing with the guinea blue dress and the check apron, linen check. Not cotton check. And the chillon. You know, the old head hangar. Oh, yes. It was fixed up nice like a hat. They didn't wear plenty. Old folks didn't wear plenty hats.
How old were you when you saw that?
I was old enough to remember. I don't remember exactly my age, but I was old enough to run off and go see Don Scrayola.
Just a little girl still going to school?
I was old enough to go and see it all right.
When did they stop it?
Well, as you say, it got so modern, so modern, so modern.
Did it last until, say, the turn of the century? Until 1900? After George was born, did they have them at home?
Oh, no. George wasn't born. I was about 13 or 14 years old.
No, honestly, you used to have that when I was a boy. You used to have what they called it. Grand Army.
Grand Army. Grand Army was on Claiborne.
Grand Army. Yeah. The memorial.
All those veterans you know.
Grand Army.
The memorial. They have something down in Chalmette now. Yeah. They didn't watch.
It was on Claiborne between Oiseline and Bayou Road. It used to be called Bayou Road Street. Then, now they call it Governor Nicholas.
Under, where did you used to sing contits? Was it in church?
In the church?
During the service or?
No, no. It was just the chorus or the priest and then that was upstairs. But in houses, or wakes, they used to sing contits. At wakes. At night, yes. Sing plenty.
The wakes would last all night.
Till four o'clock in the morning. Five o'clock in the morning.
Mrs. Zeno, you mentioned once about another son. How many children did you have? I never did. I asked George.
Oh, me? I had four solid children. One born dead.
When you hear us say son, she don't mean a son. That was a nephew. Oh, a nephew. That was a nephew. Yeah. Yeah. She didn't raise none over two years old.
No.
That was her nephew. She raised them. Yeah. Yeah. I see.
Sidney. Well. Sidney was. Sidney. Well, he died.
Sidney.
Sidney is dead about 14 years. I'm a young boy.
My granddaughter is 10 years old, 12 years old. He's been dead about 12 years. I don't know.
First cousin of my dad. Sidney.

Yeah, Sidney's date 14 years. Going on 14. How old is Shirley? What do you call him? George, baby George is 12. Well, that's Sidney died four days after her birth. She's born on Thanksgiving. Around the 2nd or the 3rd of December, somewhere around there. Because Thanksgiving, that little girl was born on Thanksgiving Day. Or the next day. And Sidney died a couple of days after.
Y'all was the only child he would raise.
The only best left. And I didn't think I would raise him. Never thought I would raise George. to the age that he is now. Well, God knows all. He knows best.
I was wondering about any of the other dances,
the quadrilles. Did you ever dance any quadrilles when you were young?
Oh, yes. When I'd go to the dances, you know. We didn't call it dance. They didn't call them dance. They called them ball.
Oh, ball.
Ball.
When you danced the quadrilles, what sort of parts did it have? Did it have four different parts?
Yeah, well, there'd be four on each side.
Yeah.
Four there and four here.
Oh, yeah. Opposite each other?
Yeah, opposite each other.
Did you call it a contradance?
No, no, not contradance. Well, maybe the Cajun called it contradance. Oh, I see.
Did you dance the contradance?
Well, the quadrilles.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Is the quadrille a kind of contradance? What do you mean by contradance when you use the word?
Oh, the quadrille, you see, we danced facing. It was really pretty.
Mm-hmm.
Really pretty.
Did you, well, was there one set of steps for the whole dance or were there different sections?
No, you see, four would get there, a man and the lady, and two there and two there, you see, and facing, like I'm facing you. Yes. That would be the same.
Yeah.
And they had two, three, four parts in the quadrille.
Oh, four parts.
Four parts. Four parts, yeah. You danced the real French by the way. Yeah.
Yeah. There's what, was it pantalon was one section? Is that right?
The Cajun called it contradance.
Contredance. Oh, I see.
Did they have any regular dance halls open to the public when you were young? How far back?
Oh, yes. Oh, yes.
I wondered, were they just the dances? They had the big balls in the homes?
Balls. The Mardi Gras carnival? Not in the, they didn't give balls in the homes.
No, but I mean the other.
In them halls, yes.
The party. Did they dance at the homes for parties or not sometimes?
Oh, yes. Oh, they danced from the time they got in till the time the musicians would take the instruments to go.
I wondered if they had any dance halls when you were young, like the Globe Hall, you know?
Oh, yes. They had L'Amitié. They had Perseverance. They had Artisans. How do they call that little hall on Robinson Street? L'Equite. L'Equite.
L'Equite.
L'Equite. L'Equite.
New hall. Artisan hall.
New hall is Artisan.
Did you go to the Mississippi Valley Hall? No.
No, that was after my time. Not in my time.
No, they had so many halls. Most of the people, most of the people of downtown, the Creole people, still there are more than they searching, you know?
L'Espérance, L'Espérance, Artisan, Perseverance, L'Equite. Sincère.
Well, where was that?
Sincère was on the clebond between Columbus. Yes. Somewhere where that church is, where that…
Between Columbus and La Hoppe.
Eh?
Between Columbus and La Hoppe.
Between Col… oh no, it was not as…
Between Calarick and Columbus.
Calarick, yes.
Yeah, where the Union is now. Yeah, on this side of… Yes. On the light side of the road.
That where they got the… they got a… a society deck. Where is it?
Where are those two on the other?
On… on… on… on… on… Progressive.

They had a hall… I can't remember the name. D'Anterial Church… Preston, Villery, Robinson and between Columbus, between St. Andes. No hallway, no dog people was allowed. From Zambia? From Zambia. Did you go to some sort of French school when you were a child?
Well, I had French teachers.
Oh, you had French teachers? Yes. Did you have sisters?
No, no, it was Miss Jarot, she's dead now. Miss Amanda Jarot.
Oh, yes.

And then my mother used to work for the Renaissance family. There was two sisters, single. They were the Mazurros then. And I was raised there with them, right there in the house. And when my mother stopped working there, then she put me with me Jarot. For French.
Oh, I see. So you got very good teaching in French.

Oh, yes. Oh, yes. The Miss Mazurros, Miss Jarot. Real French. And then after I left them, I was so Frenchy, I rather work with the French people, you know. I worked with them. It was then French, French, French. Well, I was a big girl. I didn't speak Creole at all. Just French. I went then, I went to work with the Gascones, you know. And, you know, they still didn't know nothing but Creole. And I had to speak French with them. I was born in the city of New Orleans, on St. Claude, between Columbus and Caleric.
But I wanted to get your full name. How do you spell your name? Is it the different French spelling?
Alice. Alice. A-L-I-C-E. Same as English. William. I like William. Alice William.
And the Zeno, does that have an N on the N? Is it Z-E-N-O?
Z-E-N-O. Z-E-N-O. In French, it has an N on the N. But not in English. Not in English. In French, it's Z-E-N-O-N. In English, it's Z-E-N-O.
So you spell it the English way, though, now, right? Hmm? Yeah. You get your mail the English way.
Yes. They don't pronounce Z-E-N-O no more in French. It's just in my christening paper. I believe it's N-O-N. Because it was N. No, it's N-O.
You still have your christening paper?
Oh, me, I had to have my christening paper, yes. I don't know if I got it yet. I think in that envelope.
Did you bring all of your books over, all of those books that you used to have over on St. Philip Street, did you bring them all over here?
No, I had no place to put nothing, nothing, nothing. I brought nothing but myself here.
You didn't throw those books out, I hope, did you?
I hope they didn't.
I know you had all sorts of books.
Hmm, I guess so.
What was that one book you showed me once about the American Indians? Some friend of yours wrote a book on the... Oh.
Mrs. Renshaw.
Mrs. Renshaw.
Uh, uh, Hataima. George has got it. Oh, you had that issues.
I forgot what that book was. I know you showed it to us one day.
Yes, Miss, Miss, Le Breton, Le Breton, her name. But it's Le Breton in French. So she took 42, if not longer than that, to write that book.
Well, she taught at Newcomb, didn't she? Hmm? She taught at Newcomb College, didn't she?

They still, they don't teach no more now. But they, I don't know what they are, there's something in that Newcomb and Tulane and Loyola, Loyola as they call it. Yes. Oh, those are smart people. Hmm. Hmm.
Oh, you're not taking a picture of me, I hope. No, no. No, no.

It's going to get out of the way, huh? Yeah, I think it was a deep bit. When Dick was patting you, he was one of those smart people, you see. He's one of those smart people that he's lying, I had to pat him on the back.
That's when we get out of the way. How many different languages could you read? Did you read German to you?

They read it to me. I was like all young people, foolish, giggling, wouldn't pay attention, wouldn't. But, you know, W.W. King. Yes. Gracie King. Yes. You know, they had a class all the week, every other day I believe, where Herman Gessner, which the one teaching there must be his grandson, and then Mrs. Verar and Charles Gaiare. Oh, yes. Mrs. Gerard and Charles Gaiare was French, and Capitaine de Chivarria was for Spanish, and Herman Gessner was German. So every other day they had a class, ladies would be there, Mrs. Schafferri, Mrs. LaDue, Mrs. Sam, Sam, S-E-M-M-E-S. They'd be together and they'd have, just like we're talking now, and they speak nothing but that language of the class that did to me. And I used to laugh, ask me for water and tell me thank you or something like that. So one day Mrs. Gracie told me, little girl, you have an opportunity of learning what you'll never be able to pay for. And then I reflect all that evening. I say, well, after all, Mrs. Gracie is right. I can't pay no Spanish, what's the name, teacher, neither German, French are no all right. So I begin, I begin to pay, just spoke Spanish, Capitaine de Chivarria was a Spaniard.
You can understand Spanish then too? A little. Were there many Spanish people in the city when you were young that you remember?
Plenty, they had plenty, Cubans most so. And they had several Spanish families that I knew of. Then after that, those that came would not read Spanish, they were Cubans.
Did you hear much of Spanish music when you were a girl?
Well, I don't.
On guitar or anything? Guitar, yes.
Any Spanish pieces that you remember? Yes, guitar. Plenty, guitar.

Do you have any more questions? I was wondering a little bit more about some of the other dances. If they ever charged admission at any of those halls, could anybody go? Or were there just a certain club would usually give a dance? Anybody, anybody could go, anybody. Anybody could go. Do you remember what kind of bands, when was the first time that you heard a band something like George has now? Was there any old band?
They didn't have no band like that. Nothing like that in their songs? Mm-mm. They had Chiot, Doublet, and old man Jeannot, but it wasn't like it is now.
What instruments did they play?

Well, they played, what you call it, Carmney, and LaBas Plenty. Bass. What you call them, how you call that man just? Albert Glenny. Albert Glenny. Well, he was a bass player. And old man Jeannot was a bass player. They had another bass player. But they didn't play like they play now.
Did they use any clarinets like George plays?
I don't remember any clarinet. I don't remember. La flute, violon, you lit with violin.
Do you remember any homemade instruments or things like washboards and beating on logs? I saw them on the street.
On the street. People used to play. They had a man used to play on Royal Street with washboard and made good music.
When was that? Was that before George was born?
Oh, yes, indeed. Oh, yes. They had a man with a saw and one with a washboard on the Royal Street. We used to play.
I think that, uh, we don't want to bother you all afternoon. I know you must be getting tired. But dear

segments.title: Opening reel and talk about Creole French
segments.summary: Reel 1 opens; Mrs. Zeno and the interviewers chat about how Creole French differs from standard French and Cajun, and check who is in the room.

segments.title: Trying to elicit French lullabies and songs she cannot recall
segments.summary: The interviewer asks for old French songs and lullabies; she sings fragments (My dear cousin, Mrs. Caba) but says her memory has gone.

segments.title: The Haitian revolution song learned from her grandmother
segments.summary: She sings a song of Haiti/Santo Domingo about the end of suffering and says she learned songs from her grandmother and mother.

segments.title: Her Senegalese great-grandmother and the songs she passed down
segments.summary: Her great-grandmother was brought from Senegal at eight, remembered her father's name, and sang songs for the children; Paraco translated the language.

segments.title: Cantiques and the Marie Madeleine hymn
segments.summary: Asked for cantiques, she sings 'Marie Madeleine, laissez-moi passer' but recalls little more.

segments.title: Senegalese words and phrases
segments.summary: She gives a few Senegalese words (avadra, 'good morning') and tries to recall dance songs like Kalinda.

segments.title: Lullabies she sang to her children
segments.summary: She says she sang to put her sons to sleep, cannot recall the songs, and the interviewer offers to bring tapes next time.

segments.title: Mardi Gras song 'Fum, fum' and its translation
segments.summary: She sings a Mardi Gras song Tati used to sing and translates it as a woman being told to sweep the house.

segments.title: Creole dancing, costumes and real Indians of her youth
segments.summary: She describes Creole dances and Indian dress, and real Indians who stayed at her grandmother's and sold at the Indian market.

segments.title: Songs of slavery and Fé Dodo
segments.summary: She says the St. Domingo song is about freedom, then sings a bit of 'Fé Dodo'.

segments.title: Jacques Villery collecting songs at the old folks' home
segments.summary: She recounts giving songs to young Jacques Villery at the home and discusses his family in the French Quarter.

segments.title: Reel 2: Creole words and dances before kalenda and bamboula
segments.summary: Reel 2 opens with Creole words; she discusses polka, mazurka and quadrille, kalenda as a song, and the African bamboula dance.

segments.title: Congo Square pictured and the Zolipon dance
segments.summary: Russell shows an old Congo Square picture; she says there were only trees and recalls the Zolipon dance there.

segments.title: The killing of the chief and Italians hiding in her house
segments.summary: She recalls the day the chief was killed and how her family sheltered three Italians; a song 'Downfall of a Lion' is mentioned.

segments.title: How the Congo Square dances were run and what music they had
segments.summary: She describes outdoor dances with Creole beer, singing, mule-jaw percussion and spoons, free admission.

segments.title: Globe Hall's location and George on playing there
segments.summary: They place Globe Hall near St. Claude and St. Peter; George says he played there and recalls it becoming a boxing arena and broom factory.

segments.title: White spectators, dress, and when the dances ended
segments.summary: White people came to watch; she describes the dress, says she was a girl of 13 or 14, and George recalls Grand Army events.

segments.title: Singing cantiques at wakes
segments.summary: Cantiques were sung in houses and at wakes through the night, not in church service.

segments.title: Her children and nephew Sidney
segments.summary: She says she had four children, one stillborn; George clarifies Sidney was a nephew she raised, and George was the only one she raised.

segments.title: How the quadrille was danced
segments.summary: She explains the quadrille: four couples facing, with several parts, and its relation to the contredance.

segments.title: Creole dance halls of downtown New Orleans
segments.summary: She lists halls such as L'Amitie, Perseverance, Artisans, L'Equite and Sincere, and locates them.

segments.title: French teachers and spelling of her name
segments.summary: She learned French from Miss Jarot and the Mazurro sisters, worked for French families, and spells her name Zenon in French.

segments.title: Her books, Mrs. Le Breton and language classes
segments.summary: They discuss her old books and a book on Indians by Mrs. Le Breton, then her languages class with several teachers.

segments.title: Spanish and Cuban people and guitar music
segments.summary: She says there were many Cubans and Spanish families and plenty of guitar.

segments.title: First bands, instruments and washboard players
segments.summary: She says bands were not like George's; she names early players, bass and violin, no clarinet, and street washboard and saw players.

segments.title: Closing the interview
segments.summary: Russell ends the session as she is getting tired.
